COIN: A Large-Scale Dataset for Comprehensive Instructional Video Analysis
CVPR, June 2019
Large-scale instructional-video analysis with hierarchical task and step annotations.
COIN: 11,827 videos; 180 tasks; 12 domains; 476 hours; step descriptions and temporal boundaries.
R-C3D, SSN and task-consistency variants for localization; action-segmentation baselines including TCFPN-ISBA.
Supervised step localization and action segmentation; compares standard detectors with task-consistency constraints.
mAP and mAR at temporal IoU 0.1-0.5; frame accuracy for segmentation.
Task consistency improved localization. For SSN Fusion at IoU 0.5, mAP rose from 8.12 to 9.05 and mAR from 26.79 to 29.79.
Fixed task taxonomy; YouTube availability changes; does not test free-form grouping of independent files or fairness.
Direct source of the 21 pilot clips and their task-step ground truth.
Essential
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/html/Tang_COIN_A_Large-Scale_Dataset_for_Comprehensive_Instructional_Video_Analysis_CVPR_2019_paper.html

Cross-Task Weakly Supervised Learning From Instructional Videos
CVPR, June 2019
Learning task steps with weak supervision from narration and ordered step lists while sharing knowledge across tasks.
CrossTask: about 4,700 videos; 83 tasks; 374 hours; 18 primary and 65 related tasks.
Component-sharing model; task-specific step model; DIFFRAC baseline; RGB I3D, ResNet-152 and audio VGG features.
Tests task-specific learning, cross-task sharing and parsing of previously unseen tasks.
Step recall for the 18 primary tasks; F1 on a smaller five-task comparison.
The full component-sharing model reached 22.4% average recall versus 18.6% for the task-specific model and improved 17 of 18 tasks.
Assumes an ordered step list and instructional narration; annotations focus on primary tasks; not a shuffled multi-event test.
Supports using shared action components and narration to connect related clips and transfer to new events.
High
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/html/Zhukov_Cross-Task_Weakly_Supervised_Learning_From_Instructional_Videos_CVPR_2019_paper.html

Ego4D Goal-Step: Toward Hierarchical Understanding of Procedural Activities
NeurIPS 2023
Recognizing goals, steps and substeps and their long-term hierarchical and temporal relationships.
Ego4D Goal-Step: 48,000 step segments covering 430 hours; goal annotations for 2,807 hours.
ActionFormer, EgoOnly, LSTR and VSLNet using Omnivore or egocentric video features.
Goal/step localization, online detection, open-vocabulary grounding and hierarchy ablations.
Detection mAP over tIoU 0.1-0.5; per-frame mAP; Recall@1 at IoU 0.3.
Step localization remained difficult: best test mAP was 14.0. Joint step-substep training improved grounding, but goal-step integration remained unresolved.
Egocentric single-stream video; substantial training requirements; does not cluster separate unordered media files.
Best precedent for a goal-event-step-substep hierarchy and for reporting each hierarchy level separately.
Essential
https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/7a65606fa1a6849450550325832036e5-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html
Procedural hierarchy
HT-Step: Aligning Instructional Articles with How-To Videos
NeurIPS 2023
Grounding article steps in narrated how-to videos, including steps and tasks unseen during training.
HT-Step: 122,000 segment annotations; 20,000 narrated cooking videos; about 2,300 hours; 4,958 unique steps.
ActionFormer, ActionFormer-T, UMT, VINA and MT+BCE with S3D/TimeSformer video and Word2Vec/CLIP/MPNet text features.
Strongly supervised article grounding with seen and unseen splits; tests weak ASR pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning.
Article-grounding mAP at temporal IoU 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 and averaged across thresholds.
ASR pretraining plus HT-Step labels produced the best average results: 30.2 mAP on seen tasks and 20.4 on unseen tasks.
Cooking-focused; depends on instructional articles and a step taxonomy; 73% of labels are partial matches.
Shows how transcripts, textual step descriptions and precise temporal labels can complement each other.
High
https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/9d58d85bfc041b4f901c62ba37a3f322-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html
Procedural hierarchy
Video-Mined Task Graphs for Keystep Recognition in Instructional Videos
NeurIPS 2023
Learning probabilistic relations between steps directly from video and using them to correct keystep predictions.
COIN and CrossTask for recognition; HowTo100M for representation learning.
Video-mined task graph; VideoCLIP, DistantSupervision, linear-step, autoregressive, Drop-DTW and Graph2Vid baselines.
Zero-shot keystep recognition with text, video and video-text inputs; downstream step, task and forecasting evaluations.
Frame-wise accuracy and IoU for segmentation; accuracy for classification and forecasting.
The graph improved all modality variants, with gains up to 6.5 percentage points, and improved downstream representations.
Operates within a keystep vocabulary and instructional-video distributions; does not generate arbitrary event clusters.
Most direct evidence that a learned graph can repair locally plausible but globally inconsistent step assignments.
Essential
https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/d62e65cfdba247e0cd7cac5964f9fbd9-Abstract-Conference.html

Perception Test: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Video Models
NeurIPS 2023
Broad diagnostic testing of multimodal perception under controlled real-world video scenarios.
11,600 videos; 23-second average; about 100 participants; object/point tracks, action/sound segments and video QA.
Tracking and detection baselines plus ActionFormer, Flamingo and SeViLA for temporal and video-QA tasks.
Zero-shot, few-shot and limited-fine-tuning transfer tests across six annotation types.
Task-specific IoU/Jaccard, mAP, HOTA and video-QA accuracy; combined diagnostic score.
Human video-QA performance was 91.4% versus 45.8% for the evaluated model baseline.
Mostly short, staged diagnostic scenes; separate tasks rather than end-to-end reconstruction.
Supports controlled tests, human baselines and failure analysis instead of relying only on natural videos.
High
https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/8540fba4abdc7f9f7a7b1cc6cd60e409-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html
Temporal reasoning
TempCompass: Do Video LLMs Really Understand Videos?
arXiv, 1 March 2024
Measuring whether video LLMs understand temporal changes rather than exploiting single frames or language priors.
7,540 instructions across action, speed, direction, attribute change and event-order aspects using conflicting clips.
Eight video LLMs, including Video-LLaVA, LLaMA-VID and VideoChat2; three image LLMs; GPT-3.5-based answer evaluator.
Multiple choice, yes/no, caption matching and caption generation on controlled conflicting video pairs or triplets.
Accuracy and answer-match rate by temporal aspect and task format.
Evaluated video LLMs showed weak temporal perception, and several failed to consistently exceed random baselines across formats.
Short stock clips and benchmark-specific questions; model set reflects 2024 availability; no event hierarchy.
Directly motivates testing event order with clips that share static content but differ temporally.
Essential
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00476
Temporal reasoning
TimeChat: A Time-sensitive Multimodal Large Language Model for Long Video Understanding
CVPR, June 2024
Timestamp-aware localization and reasoning over videos of different durations.
TimeIT: 125,000 instruction-tuning instances across six temporal tasks; evaluated on YouCook2, QVHighlights and Charades-STA.
TimeChat with timestamp-aware frame encoder, sliding video Q-Former and LLM; compared with prior video LLMs.
Zero-shot dense captioning, temporal grounding and highlight detection; optional transcript input.
F1 and CIDEr; HIT@1 and mAP; Recall@1 at temporal IoU thresholds.
Reported gains include +9.2 F1 and +2.8 CIDEr on YouCook2, +5.8 HIT@1 on QVHighlights and +27.5 R@1 at IoU 0.5 on Charades-STA.
Focuses on moments within one video, not grouping separate files; practical access may require local model deployment.
Supports timestamped evidence and a transcript ablation for long or ambiguous event clips.
High
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/html/Ren_TimeChat_A_Time-sensitive_Multimodal_Large_Language_Model_for_Long_Video_CVPR_2024_paper.html
Temporal reasoning
VTimeLLM: Empower LLM to Grasp Video Moments
CVPR, June 2024
Teaching a video LLM to identify fine-grained temporal boundaries and describe multiple events.
Training combines image-text alignment, boundary-aware multi-event videos and instruction data; evaluation uses ActivityNet Captions and Charades-STA.
VTimeLLM-7B and VTimeLLM-13B built on Vicuna 1.5 with three-stage training and LoRA.
Temporal video grounding and dense video captioning against video-LLM baselines.
mIoU; Recall@1 at IoU 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7; SODA_c, CIDEr and METEOR.
VTimeLLM-7B substantially outperformed similarly sized video LLMs on temporal grounding and dense captioning; scaling to 13B gave smaller additional gains.
Designed for moments inside one video; results depend on specialized staged training and generated instruction data.
Provides metrics for temporal boundaries and event captions, useful when the pilot expands beyond three fixed clips.
Medium
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/html/Huang_VTimeLLM_Empower_LLM_to_Grasp_Video_Moments_CVPR_2024_paper.html
Temporal reasoning
Video-MME: The First-Ever Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark of Multi-modal LLMs in Video Analysis
CVPR, June 2025
Comprehensive evaluation of multimodal LLMs across video duration, domain and input modality.
Video-MME: videos from 11 seconds to one hour; six domains and 30 subfields; video, subtitle and audio conditions.
Commercial and open models including Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4V, VITA, VILA and LLaVA-NeXT-Video.
Multiple-choice evaluation by duration and domain, with and without subtitle/audio inputs.
Average answer accuracy overall and by duration, domain and modality condition.
Gemini 1.5 Pro scored 75.0% and GPT-4o 71.9%. Subtitles/audio helped, while performance declined as duration increased.
Multiple-choice QA does not evaluate clustering, ordering or generated hierarchy; model rankings age quickly.
Provides the strongest template for model comparison, duration analysis and multimodal ablations.
Essential
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/html/Fu_Video-MME_The_First-Ever_Comprehensive_Evaluation_Benchmark_of_Multi-modal_LLMs_in_CVPR_2025_paper.html
Fairness evaluation
Casual Conversations: A Dataset for Measuring Fairness in AI
CVPR Workshops, June 2021
Measuring model robustness across age, gender, apparent skin tone and lighting in consented videos.
More than 45,000 videos from 3,011 participants across multiple U.S. states; about 15 videos per person.
State-of-the-art apparent age and gender classification systems.
Reports classification behavior across self-reported age/gender, annotated apparent skin tone and low-light conditions.
Classification accuracy and error patterns disaggregated by demographic and lighting groups.
The evaluations reveal that aggregate performance can conceal substantial variation across participant groups and conditions.
Speaking-face videos and U.S.-focused collection; fairness attributes are limited; no event or temporal reconstruction task.
Provides a consent-aware protocol for subgroup reporting in a later smartphone-video fairness dataset.
High
https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021W/RCV/html/Hazirbas_Casual_Conversations_A_Dataset_for_Measuring_Fairness_in_AI_CVPRW_2021_paper.html
Fairness evaluation
FACET: Fairness in Computer Vision Evaluation Benchmark
ICCV 2023; released 31 August 2023
Standardized intersectional fairness evaluation for common person-related computer-vision tasks.
FACET: 32,000 images; 50,000 people; 52 person classes; expert labels for demographic and other attributes.
State-of-the-art classification, object detection, instance segmentation and visual-grounding models.
Compares task performance across single demographic attributes and intersections of multiple attributes.
Task metrics such as classification accuracy, detection/segmentation performance and subgroup performance gaps.
Models across all four task families exhibit performance disparities across demographic attributes and their intersections.
Still images, perceived attributes and evaluation-only licensing; no temporal or multimodal event reasoning.
Provides the clearest reporting pattern for intersectional performance gaps and sample-size disclosure.
High
https://ai.meta.com/research/publications/facet-fairness-in-computer-vision-evaluation-benchmark/

values: Research synthesis and pilot implications
The literature supports a component-based evaluation of grouping, temporal order, hierarchy and later fairness analysis.
Review coverage
Count
Reading priority
Count
Papers reviewed
Essential
Procedural hierarchy
High
Temporal reasoning
Medium
Fairness evaluation
Key evidence
Temporal structure helps correct local mistakes; current video LLMs still struggle with controlled temporal reasoning; audio and transcripts can improve results; duration increases difficulty.
Research gap

Inference from this targeted review: no reviewed paper jointly tests blind clustering of independent clips, within-cluster ordering, generated hierarchy and fairness breakdown in one general-purpose multimodal model evaluation.
Immediate experiment
Use the existing 21 blind clips. Run each accessible model with a fixed JSON schema, at least three prompt variants, and separate video-only and video-plus-transcript conditions when supported.
Recommended metrics

Grouping: pairwise precision, recall and F1 plus Adjusted Rand Index. Ordering: pairwise precedence, exact three-clip sequence and Kendall's tau. Hierarchy: blinded human ratings. Report each component separately.
Fairness boundary

The current COIN pilot cannot support a fairness claim because it lacks controlled demographic labels. Add matched demographic and recording-context groups only after the reconstruction protocol is stable.
Scope note
This is a targeted review for experiment design, not a systematic review. The full paper details and primary links are in the Literature Matrix sheet.
